7.8.m: And summoning all the Dānavas headed by Vipracitti, / he said: 'Go swiftly, bind that lion, and bring him before me, / O leaders of the Daityas! He must not be killed by any means; / this lion cub will become a plaything for my queen.' / Having heard this, all the asuras, led by Vipracitti, / went together to the pleasure garden and saw Nṛsiṃha standing there. / Standing far off, they cast nets; Mādhava cut them to pieces. / Then the maned lion thoroughly routed the Dānavas. / Thereupon those Daityas, their comrades slain, went despondently / to the presence of the king of the Dānavas and recounted everything then. / Then the mighty King Hiraṇyakaśipu himself, enraged, / mounted his chariot, armed, and rushed furiously against Nṛsiṃha. / That mountain-like chariot, equipped with weapons, was whirled around / and quickly hurled down by the king of lions; it was reduced to powder upon the earth. / Then, with his chariot broken, his eyes red with rage, the Daitya / violently tore up a tree and flung it at Nṛsiṃha. / But when that tree fell upon the body of the lion king, / it was shattered to dust like a lump of clay dashed against a rock. / Then seizing Hiraṇyakaśipu all at once, / that lion struck him with his palm and quickly deprived him of his life. / Giving a great lion's roar, with his adamantine claws the omnipresent Lord, / Hari, tore open the Daitya's chest, which resembled a great mountain.

When that great Daitya was slain by Viṣṇu, O son of Śakti, / those Dānavas who were not killed entered Rasātala.
Śakra once again obtained the supreme kingdom of heaven, free of thorns, / and all the celestials returned to their own realms. / Then the trident-bearing God whose banner bears the bull arrived, / having been petitioned by the gods, O Vyāsa, as I told you,
to cause Viṣṇu, of wondrous deeds, to relinquish his leonine form. / Becoming then a Śarabha resembling a peak of the Himālaya,

with four legs growing from his back, sharp fangs, and great strength, / he went near Narasiṃha and roared with focused intent. / Then seeing the Śarabha arrived before him, / the lion, filled with great wrath, struck him with his palm.
Though struck by that lion, the Śarabha was not agitated at all. / Then, having struck the Śarabha of adamantine body and great strength,
he himself experienced pain by the mere touch of that great-souled one. / Then Viṣṇu, meditating for a long time, realized that Śaṅkara had arrived.
Bowing to him with his head, he began to praise him thus: / 'Homage to Śarva, to Rudra, to the commander of the army, and to the bestower of peace!
Homage to the supreme God and to the supreme Brahman! / Homage to Time, to the one whose form is Yama, and indeed to the Rod of Death!
Homage to the destroyer of the world, and to the one who takes away time in due time! / Homage to the bearer of the Pināka, and to the holder of fierce arrows!
To the fierce one, to Vāmadeva, and to the lord of all yogas! / Homage to the master of knowledge, homage to the lord of sacred lore!

To the master of the three worlds, and homage to the lord of the worlds! / Homage to the bestower of yoga upon me, and likewise to the granter of divine power, / to the bestower of invulnerability, and likewise to the bestower of what cannot be conquered! / O Lord, I am established in you, devoted to you, having you as my supreme refuge. / I have taken refuge in you; be ever gracious to me!' / Whoever listens to this constantly, pure and of restrained mind, / having attained the world of Rudra, becomes a leader of the God's gaṇas.
Reciting it, hearing it, and constantly remembering it / brings wealth, brings fame, grants long life, leads to heaven, and destroys sins.
Sanatkumāra said: / Thus praised by Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe / addressed this supremely revered word to Hṛṣīkeśa:
'To you, O Viṣṇu, has been granted by me this auspicious, meritorious boon: / that you, who were clinging to an unnatural form, are restored to your own natural state.'

7.8.m: […] / You, that Viṣṇu of great splendour, having always received a boon from me, / [you] whom the ocean gave birth to on its shore as an animal: / all your work has been accomplished, Hiraṇyakaśipu has been slain. / Come, return to your own auspicious, exceedingly wondrous nature.’ / Then that best of śarabhas stepped upon that lion with his feet, / and once again united Keśava with his divine body. / Having thus granted to Viṣṇu the boon of destroying demons, he whose banner bears the bull, / saying, ‘Return to your natural state,’ vanished right there. / Having granted that matchless boon to Viṣṇu, the creator of the world, / the ability to destroy demons, being drunk in by the eyes of the women of heaven's city, / bearing a chest radiant like a dark cloud, the trident-bearer, / praised by the foremost sages, went to his own abode. / Thus in the Skandapurāṇa, in the story of Hiraṇyakaśipu, ends the seventy-first chapter, entitled ‘The Account of the Deliverance of Narasiṃha Accomplished by the Śarabha’.

Vyāsa said: / Lord, knower of all yoga, this excellent narrative has been heard. / I wish to hear what happened thereafter, O best of sages. / When he whose banner bears the bull had then removed the lion form of Viṣṇu, / what else did the wise one do? This I desire to know. / Sanatkumāra said: / Having brought Viṣṇu back to his own origin, the god of gods, Bhava, / then wandered upon Mount Mandara together with the goddess, full of great splendour. / Delighting in the charming forest regions and the mountain's cascades, / the lord of gods adorned them as he roamed all around.
[…] / Knowing that the imperishable god Śaṅkara was fond of gazing at the forest, / two seasons, autumn and spring, both appeared there together. / Then all the trees and lakes all around / suddenly and simultaneously shed diverse kinds of flowers.
Charming ponds were covered with blue and white lotuses, / frequented by swarms of bees, / and inhabited by swans and cranes.

Jasmines swiftly became rich with fragrance, together with campaka flowers, / aśokas, sweet-scented blossoms, and atimuktaka creepers.
Pleasant breezes bearing all fragrances approached the god together. / Beholding that excellent forest strewn with the flowers of all seasons,
the lord of the gods, the master of the world, taking the flowers himself, / with a joyful heart adorned the goddess, the daughter of the snowy mountain,
and Nandīśvara who was standing nearby, and himself, the lord of the gods. / Then, having bowed to the lord of gods, out of love Pārvatī
spoke this word, she the imperishable mother of the entire world: / ‘O god whose banner bears the bull, so that a son born of my body will come to be,
possessing your valour, your power, and revered by all the gods, / act accordingly, O Mahādeva, if you have affection for me.’
Addressed thus by the goddess, the god of gods, the three-eyed one, / full of great splendour, spoke thus, wishing to do what was pleasing to the goddess:
‘So be it, O ruler of gods! I shall make this petition of yours fruitful, / O Īśānī, so that you may have such a son,

dreadful meteors fell, and the directions became utterly terrifying. / Thus the earth was terrified by portents, even though it was for an auspicious cause.
[The Earth] went for refuge to Viṣṇu, and having gone, reported her distress: / 'O God, many terrible portents have arisen exceedingly.
Greatly agitated by this, I have come to you today for refuge.' / Then the lord Viṣṇu proclaimed this to all the gods:
Thereupon all the gods, led by Bṛhaspati, / gathered together in one place and held discussions of many kinds.
Then the son of Aṅgiras, endowed with great intellect, spoke these words: / 'This Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, the God of gods, the three-eyed,
the greatly radiant one, has united with the daughter of the Himālaya for the sake of a son / by the yoga of Parameṣṭhin for a divine thousand years.
As he remains united with Pārvatī, terrible portents have arisen from it, / terrors for the world; what else should be contemplated here?
Let us all go together to praise the bull-bannered [god] with devotion, / so that, O lords of the gods, the son born of the goddess's body may be averted.

And your word cannot be transgressed; this is an extreme hardship for me. / I shall enter like a messenger, O gods; I shall perform a great daring deed.' / Having said this, he quickly went to the abode of the matted-haired god.

Nandin replied this to him: ‘This boon is indeed difficult to grant. / You will not be able to see that lord of the gods absorbed in union [with the goddess],
the great lord together with the goddess, the imperishable creator of the world. / Even so, O fire, this boon must certainly be granted by me to you. / Go, having become very subtle, hard to perceive, O fire; / enter and come out quickly, your act of arrival unnoticed.’ / Permitted by Nandin, fire, filled with joy, / having become a light most subtle together with a ray of the sun,

The gods together, led by Brahmā, became silent.
Then in their midst, the fire said to the lord of the world:
'Offer this supreme fiery splendor into me, O god, protector of the three worlds.'
Then Bhava offered that supreme fiery splendor of his own into the fire.
Having offered it all into him, the supreme lord was pleased.
'Choose a boon, O fire,' said Śaṃkara.

Then the fire bowed to the lord and requested boons from the almighty:
'I would wish this son of yours to be renowned by my name.
May I be beyond the reach of curses, and may I see you constantly.
May I bear this with ease and release it [safely], O Śaṃkara.
Even while devouring everything, may I remain untainted, and let there be no sin for me.
May the gods and sacrifices find their support in me, O bearer of the trident!
May I be a lord of beings, and may I indeed be Paśupati.
May I be your body, your form, and dependent on you.'

'I desire this boon, O lord of gods, as it is being granted by you.'
Saying 'So be it,' the almighty granted all that to the fire.
Then, dismissing the gods, the god of gods, whose emblem is the bull,
entered the chamber again, and the goddess addressed him:
'Where did you go and then return here so quickly, O lord of the three worlds?
What was that very urgent matter on account of which you went outside?'
Then the lord of gods spoke to Pārvatī, whose face was angry:
'I went quickly, O goddess, having been petitioned by the gods, O beloved,
who were standing outside, O lotus-petal-eyed one, full of devotion and deeply distressed.'
Then the goddess said to the god, the lord of the entire universe:
'How, O god, did you know that the denizens of heaven had come and stood outside,
terrified? And who told you, O lord?'
The god of gods said:
'Having entered, O goddess, and stood upon a jeweled pillar,
the fire, praising me, announced all the gods who were standing outside.

named Bhadrotpala, near Hemaśṛṅga.

7.8.m:
Therefore, grant this boon: so that a son may not be conceived in the womb of the goddess,
and yet a praiseworthy son may come to be."
Then, O lady, that wondrous fiery splendor was cast into the fire by me for the sake of a son.
Your glorious son will have six heads and twelve eyes.'
Hearing his word, the mountain-born goddess cursed the immortals:
'Since a son in my body was not desired by those wicked ones,
therefore those gods shall not obtain a son in their own wives.
And the earth also, bewildered, her senses impaired by my curse,
having obtained many husbands, shall never obtain a son.'
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the goddess fell silent after cursing the gods along with Indra,
[she who is] sacred, known by the name Kaiṭabhā, granter of many boons.

7.8.m:
On the golden peak of the Vindhya mountain the auspicious Girijā then took up Her abode;
that is indeed a holy sanctuary, and [there is] a stone named Ramaṇā.
The man who approaches it, O Vyāsa, becomes a leader of Gaṇas upon death.
Then all the gods arrived there along with Agni,
pale, afflicted with agony, bearing embryos, and filled with shame.
Nandī announced to Śaṅkara those [gods] who stood at the door.
Having entered with his permission, the gods said to the Lord:
"We are not able to endure this splendor, O Lord of the three worlds!
Save us, O Lord of the realm of the gods, so that we may become free of fever!
Moreover, the asura Andhaka is performing exceedingly severe austerity,
and from that, O Lord, a very great danger threatens us, O all-pervading one!"

7.8.m:
The God of gods said:
"Let there be no fear for you, O gods! I will slay Andhaka,
the excellent son of Hiraṇyākṣa, who has displayed his prowess against you.
And go to the extensive forest situated in the middle of Meru,
holy and twelve yojanas in extent, known by the name Śaravaṇa.
There, O foremost among gods, bursting through your bellies,
that supreme, blazing energy of mine will come forth.
And your bellies, O best of gods, will turn to gold."
Then, having heard his word and having bowed their heads to Bhava,
they went to glorious Meru and that auspicious Śaradhāna [forest],
where, bursting their bellies, that splendor then emerged,
resembling the fire at the end of an era, unbearable to be seen by gods and asuras.
And Meru immediately became glorious and exceedingly charming.
That supreme energy of Maheśvara turned everything golden.
A celestial wind blew, carrying the perfume of flowers of all seasons.
And the bursting incisions in their bellies turned completely into gold.
In heaven, celestial drums sounded of their own accord, unstruck.
Showers of fragrant flowers fell in abundance,
and from invisible beings arose the sound of reverent greetings.
Seeing and hearing such marvels, the best of the gods,
having gone to the wielder of the Pināka, delighted, and reported everything, O you of noble vows,
dismissed by Sthāṇu, went to their own worlds with joyful faces.

7.8.m:
Having heard this excellent speech spoken by the gods full of joy,
pleased in her heart, having learned of the impending birth of her son,
the goddess, granter of boons to the gods, mother of yoga, the creator,
remained there and felt satisfaction in her heart, her lotus feet touched by the heads of the gods.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, named 'The Impending Birth of Skanda', in the Skandapurāṇa.
Vyāsa said:
Whose son was that Andhaka? What was his valor, what was his prowess?
And how was he slain in battle? Tell me all of this!
Sanatkumāra said:
Listen, O Vyāsa of great intellect, to all this as it happened!
I will tell you the entire ancient story of Andhaka, O twice-born one.

7.8.m:
From Diti were born two sons of Kaśyapa, the two Daityas:
Hiraṇyakaśipu was the elder, and Hiraṇyākṣa was his younger brother.
The elder there was the king at that time, Hiraṇyakaśipu.
When that hero was slain by the wise Narasiṃha,
Hiraṇyākṣa became the king, revered by all the Daityas.
Sonless, he performed austerity for the sake of a son: such is the sacred tradition.
Having reached Śaṅkukarṇa at the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean,
that son of Diti performed austerity to see the Lord who wields the Pināka.
Vyāsa said:
How did that divine, pure, world-renowned sacred field of Maheśa,
Śaṅkukarṇa, which accomplishes all goals, come to be?
You should explain to me what its fruit and wealth of religious merit are.
Sanatkumāra said:
Long ago indeed, the blessed Lord, with matted hair, blue and red [in hue],
came to the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds.

7.8.m:
He began to perform an austerity unimaginable to gods and asuras.
Then, in all ten directions, for the sake of protection, the Lord of the world
stationed gaṇapas by the thousands, headed by Nikumbha.
Śaṅkukarṇa had huge fangs, thick eyes, a thick nose,
short legs and hands, a gaping mouth, and a terrifying form,
covered in a tiger's pelt, with a leopard's skin as an upper garment.
Having called near that very mighty leader of the Gaṇas known as Śaṅkukarṇa,
the Blessed One said this:
"Along with your leaders of the Gaṇas, so that the gods may not enter,
guard the forest accordingly, dear child, for as long as this vow of mine lasts."

7.8.m:
Having thus arranged protection, Mahādeva, whose banner bears a bull,
performed great, terrible, and exceedingly difficult austerity there.
Then all the gods, led by Śakra, arrived there.
Turned back by Śaṅkukarṇa, they did not advance a step further.
The gods said:
"O Gaṇa-chiefs, we have arrived on a mission to see the god
Śarva, the fierce one, with matted hair; therefore reveal him, O sinless ones!
Agitated, not seeing him, we perish, O lords of the Pramathas!"
Śaṅkukarṇa said:
"The Lord cannot be seen by you gods in any way.
Perform austerity, may good betide you, and then you will see Śaṅkara!"
The gods said:
"Lest there be destruction of the worlds, O leader of the Gaṇas of great splendor,
grant us passage for this reason; grant your favor to us, O Lord!"

7.8.m:
Śaṅkukarṇa said:
"Let the worlds perish, or you yourselves—entrance is not granted.
Even if they are destroyed, the Lord, the master of the world, will create them again.
He alone is the creator of beings; he likewise is their destroyer.
Who, O gods, could destroy the worlds without that all-pervading Lord?
We do not grant entrance; our command is that of the Supreme Lord."
Having been addressed thus, the gods reflected and went to the assembly of Brahmā.
Then those best of gods reported [the matter] to Brahmā.
Then Brahmā said to the gods: "Once more, O gods, with me,
go to the commanders of the gaṇas, so that I may restore you [to favor]."
Then the gods, together with Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
came again to that very place where Śaṅkara was staying.
Then that lord of the gaṇas stopped them once more—
Śaṅkukarṇa, the chief of the gaṇas, blazing as if with fiery energy.
Then Brahmā spoke to him these soothing words endowed with purpose:

"O gods, this prostration of yours is not greater to me [than my duty];
Śambhu's command is superior; there is no entrance whatsoever.
When forbidden, O Brahmā, and appointed for protection,
how can we grant entrance, having transgressed the command of Īśa?"
Having heard those words of that great-souled lord of the gaṇas,
Brahmā went aside, filled with utter shame.
Then, seeing the Grandfather filled with shame,
all the gods, enraged and their limbs filled with fury, said to the lord of the gaṇas:

Indeed, the one whose banner bears the bull will not praise you for speaking so falsely.
Furthermore, O gaṇa, do not show such disrespect to us;
prepared as we are today, we will not leave you with your life!"
Hearing their words, Śaṅkukarṇa, filled with wrath,
enraged, looked askance at the gods and said:
"Are you my elders, O rulers of the immortals, that I should fear you?
It was only having propitiated Śaṅkara that you attained excellent divinity!

7.8.m:
You, even though best among immortals, are merely gaṇas of the Lord of the gods;
we too are master-yogins, commanders of the gaṇas belonging to that wielder of the trident.
You denizens of heaven are our equals, or even inferior,
because we see the Lord of the gods and attend upon him.
Therefore, we are to be revered by all the gods and are always superior.
Behold, enter fearlessly, O immortals,
so that today you shall see the terrible power of the lords of the gaṇas!
Whatever strength you have, whatever yoga, whatever austerity, and whatever effort—
display all of that, and then you shall see my power!"
Hearing his words, all the gods, thoroughly arrogant,
swiftly took up their weapons and rushed at Śaṅkukarṇa.

With their power checked, all those foremost of gods
were unable to take a step, and stood motionless like pillars.
When the gods were restrained, Viṣṇu, best among strikers,
rushed with speed toward Śaṅkukarṇa, the lord of the gaṇas.
Then that mighty one paralyzed Viṣṇu's body by means of yoga.
Employing yoga once more, Viṣṇu, endowed with sovereign majesty,
fought with Śaṅkukarṇa, and he fought back against him.
Between those two lords of yoga who were concentrated in contemplation, O best of sages,
a tremendous battle took place, purely through yoga, with one another.

7.8.m:
Having restrained Viṣṇu, that lord of the gaṇas, dear to Śarva,
most wondrous, fought with my father by means of yoga.
Employing subtle yoga, Brahmā then entered the gross elements.
Into whatever gross element Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, entered,
right there in front he beheld Śaṅkukarṇa standing.
Leaving the gross elements, the lord entered the subtle elements;
then the Grandfather entered the senses, the principles, and the states of being.
Everywhere, that yogic soul beheld the exceedingly powerful Śaṅkukarṇa
with a massive head, established in supreme yoga.

7.8.m:
[Apparatus and page number] / “Fie on my life as a blind man! Death alone is better for me, / who, blind, cannot see my home, relations, and kinsmen!
Blessed are those men in the world who walk about by themselves, unperturbed, / having seen face to face their relatives, and conversing with them happily!
There may be use for a clod of earth, for grass, or even for a corpse, / but not for me, though favored! Fie on me, a doer of unpropitious deeds!
Out of love for his son, this father, the daitya, always protects me. / Though I am fit to be killed, depleting his treasury, he does not kill me.
Deluded by affection, he does not know this agony of mine. / I shall myself do what is to be done by the wisest!
Undertaking great austerity, I shall surely become possessed of sight!” / Having thus resolved in many ways, the very wise blind man,
having taken leave of his father together with his mother and bowed to him, / resolute and determined, the wise one departed for austerity.
While being watched for a long time by his father, whose eyes and face were flooded with grief and whose soul was pained with sorrow, / and by his mother, whose face streamed with repeated tears, / crying out in distress at that acute absence from their sight full of anguish and grief, sighing, / meditating upon the god, the lord of Umā, Andhaka went forth from his home to perform austerity.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, entitled ‘Departure for Austerity,’ in the story of Andhaka in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.8.m:
Sanatkumāra said: / Having spoken thus, O descendant of Parāśara, he of great strength / fed on wind for a year, free from weariness,
bathing at the three junctures of the day, making offerings into the fires, / devoted to worshipping the gods, and intent on silent recitation and oblations.
As each full year passed, cutting from his own limbs a kārṣika measure / portion of flesh, the great asura then offered it into the fire.
In this manner a thousand divine years passed for him, O best of sages, / as he daily offered his own flesh.
That asura, pale as a conch, a pearl necklace, water, nectar, a kunda flower, and the moon, / became reduced to mere bones and veins, remaining solely steadfast in austerity.
Endowed with that austerity, he of restrained mind then rendered / the sun, moon, planets, and stars devoid of luster.

[Apparatus and page number] / Just like that sun, he illuminated [the world] with his radiance; / he dried up ponds, rivers, wells, and lakes.
Then, through his austerity, Andhaka arrested the wind; / the perfected beings could not move in the sky, and aerial chariots fell down.
Seeing the nature of that austerity of his, Śakra, with hundreds of obstacles, / quickly acted, but he [Andhaka] underwent no perturbation.
Then Brahmā approached him and said to the Dānava Andhaka:
“O great Asura! A terrible austerity has been performed by you, O one of great might!
I am pleased with you, O mighty-armed one! Gain your sight, O one of noble vows! (16)
May your body return to its natural state, just as it was before, O Asura!
And speak another boon further, which remains in your heart.” (17)

Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having gained his sight and with his body uninjured,
he bowed down directly and spoke to Brahmā, the creator of the worlds. (18)
Andhaka said:
“O Blessed One, if you are pleased, if my austerity has been accomplished,
[grant me] matchlessness in battle against the deities, O Grandfather! (19)
Great strength, magical powers, and likewise immortality as well—
this I desire, O Lord of the gods, if you are a giver of boons to me.” (20)
Sanatkumāra said:
Hearing that statement of his, the powerful Blessed One laughed
and addressed the son of Hiraṇyākṣa once more with auspicious words: (21)
“I do not grant immortality to a Daitya, O delight of Diti!
Let it have an exception; speak the alternative yourself.” (22)

Andhaka said:
“If there be a woman who is the mother of the universe, if I do not bow to her,
then let my death occur; otherwise, I am devoid of death.” (23)
Brahmā said:
“Let it be so for you, just as has been spoken by you today!
Be known by the name Andhaka, and you shall attain fame in the world.” (24)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus to Andhaka, the thorn in the side of the gods,
the Blessed One went to his own abode, and Andhaka ceased [his austerity]. (25)
Having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, worshipped the god according to rule,
offered oblation into the fire, and taken leave of the ascetic grove, the wise
lord of the Daityas went to his father’s presence along with his companions. (26)
With a glad heart from austerity, of great might, his desires fulfilled, bringing joy to the enemies of the gods,
the radiant one, resembling an agitated raincloud, went once again to his father’s presence. (27)
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter named ‘Attainment of the Boon by Andhaka’ in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.8.m:
Having gone not very far into a forest with aśoka and campaka trees,
the glorious one approached his son, like a second moon approaching Budha. (4)
Seeing his son successful, the lord of the Dānavas rejoiced;
embracing him out of affection and smelling his head repeatedly, [he asked]: (5)
‘How, at what time, and what boons were obtained by you?’
Thus questioned, he recounted everything just as it happened without remainder. (6)
Hearing of his grant of boons and likewise his majesty,
those tiger-like Asuras roared like oceans. (7)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, seating his son Andhaka upon his chariot,
Hiraṇyākṣa, along with those companions, quickly entered his own city. (8)
Accompanied by his son, the Daitya shone, his heart fulfilled,
like the sun moving into a zodiacal sign together with Saturn. (9)
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having entered, the lord of the Daityas addressed his circle of friends,
just as an Adhvaryu priest stationed at a sānnāyya offering speaks to the other priests: (10)
Hiraṇyākṣa said:
“Hear what duty, long kept in my heart, is now
to be carried out with all of you possessing formidable prowess! (11)
It was formerly resolved by me that when Andhaka returns here having achieved his purpose,
I shall celebrate the Kaumudī festival in this city. (12)
And I shall celebrate the radiant divine night of the god who destroys sacrifice—
let all of that be done without hesitation! (13)

Let it be proclaimed in this city, at crossroads and in assembly halls,
that by my command there shall be fifteen days of the Kaumudī festival. (14)
For just as long, let there be for me the divine nights of the god.
And the lords of the Daityas and powerful Dānavas who are friends (15)
in all directions—let them too assemble here and make merry;
and the auspicious brahmins who are on our side, Śukra and the rest, (16)
the Nāgas, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and humans—
let all of them too assemble and rejoice with me.” (17)
Sanatkumāra said:
Addressed thus by the wise Hiraṇyākṣa, those lords of the Daityas
then did everything just as spoken by the enemy of the gods. (18)

They swiftly dispatched messengers along with Dānavas to the Daityas
as well as to the other factions on their side, O son of Śakti! (19)
“The mighty king Hiraṇyākṣa invites you;
accompanied by your circles of friends, go, being desirous of seeing him.” (20)
And the herald, wrapped in new, unwashed garments, splendidly adorned,
mounted upon an intoxicated white elephant, made the proclamation. (21)
"Victorious is King Hiraṇyākṣa, the glorious lord of Daityas! / Slain are all the haters of Daityas and enemies of the Dānavas!
For the victory of Diti's sons and for the terror of the Ādityas, / beginning tomorrow morning, the king proclaims to you the Kaumudī festival
and the night dedicated to God Rudra, which destroys the gods! / Let the city be made ready with well-swept and smeared streets!

7.8.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
Then on that Kaumudī [full moon night], the Daityas and Dānavas,
with impassioned minds, sported along with their women like gods residing in heaven. / 1
There a woman of beautiful limbs held a divine lotus over her face,
as if to protect her lotus face from fear of the moon. / 2
Another, intoxicated, approached and struck her lover with her foot,
as the cool-rayed [moon touches] an open autumn lotus with its ray. / 3
Other noble women, unfamiliar with the royal highways,
seeing the ground paved with crystal, took off their sandals. / 4
And others, O best of brahmins, suspecting water,
pulled up their garments and walked on the royal highways, seeing the ground inlaid with gems. / 5
One woman, abandoned by her lover who had departed captivated by another,
left the house and, touched by the moonbeams, fell down, languid with love. / 6
And having fallen, that noble woman spoke thus to the moon:
"Again you burn me with your sharp rays as if I were a lotus! / 7
Indeed you revive the herbs scorched by the sun;
why then do you not truly revive me, who am burned by love?" / 8

7.8.m:
[Critical apparatus]

Some charming women, swinging other women on swings,
appeared like reflections of the moon on water, their forms trembling with the ripples. / 9
Some Daityas of great strength sang together with women,
just as Gandharvas [sing] with Apsarases in the Nandana grove. / 8.76.10
In some places the royal highway shone, crowded with numerous women,
like that bright, divine path of the gods, wondrous in the sky. / 11
Here and there, the sound of anklets and girdles and cuckoos
pleased the ear of the listener, inflaming graceful passion. / 12
Here and there, O Vyāsa, was heard the sweet voice of women
devoted to lovemaking with their lovers, confusing the heart. / 13
Thus, O Vyāsa, that festival was varied and wondrous,
increasing the affection, happiness, and trust of the Dānavas at that time. / 14

And three crores of the mighty Nivātakavacas.
All these enemies of the gods, when counted, amounted to sixty crores.
Excluding their allies: men and serpents,
rākṣasas and piśācas, yakṣas and birds—
even of these, O Vyāsa, there were twenty crores counted.
Having entered that assembly hall, all those enemies of the gods, filled with pride,
shone like monsoon rainclouds with lightning and meteors.
They were like thundering clouds, like smoking mountains,
bellowing like buffaloes, like inauspicious comets,
like unleashed portents, like venomous serpents,
like maddened elephants, like rushing winds.
To humiliate the gods, they stood filling that assembly hall.
Then the doorkeeper, having approached, spoke this to the king:
To the young [king] seated comfortably upon his throne, O Vyāsa,
having first bowed with his head, going down on his knees to the ground,

7.8.m:
his hands properly folded in supplication, [speaking] words of smooth syllables and diction:
'May the master conquer, the bringer of victory to all the asuras!
All have arrived at the assembly, headed by Prahrāda and Vipracitti.
Let this be known; you should do whatever else is fitting.'
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, hearing that all the enemies of the gods had arrived at the assembly hall,
the king suddenly stood up, like the banner of Indra at a festival.
Wearing a diadem, with large tusks, hair like muñja grass, and a mighty jaw,
with a mouth torn wide to his ears, his head like a great parasol,
with arms reaching his knees, round eyes, tawny eyes, and body hair standing on end,
with a frame hard as a thunderbolt, a great yogin of mighty power.
He shone brilliantly with his diadem, like the sunrise with the sun;
his chest adorned with an excellent necklace, like a cloud with a flight of cranes.
Accompanied by his sons, O Vyāsa, he went forth like the personified Himavat.
Then that best among kings of the dānavas, his earrings flashing with multi-colored gems,
entered the assembly packed with bull-like asuras and daityas, like the sky filled with risen planets.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, named 'The Entry into the Assembly of Hiraṇyākṣa', in the Skandapurāṇa.

Sanatkumāra said:
Having gone to that assembly, O Vyāsa, he beheld the daityas and dānavas
arrived before him, like Indra [beholding] rutting rainclouds in the monsoon season.
When he entered, all the enemies of the gods
stood up and shouted 'Victory!', as the Vedas [praise] the Grandfather [Brahmā].
'Do not rise,' the lord of the asuras said to all of them,
having attained the fivefold māyā, like a serpent [mastering] wind-dwellers.
Going before them, the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa shone,
like a rutting great elephant in the midst of a herd of calves.

Seated on the throne, that king of the enemies of the gods shone
like a great cloud accompanied by cranes upon reaching the peak of Meru.
And the asuras sat down in complete silence,
like towering dark clouds ready to release water in season.
Sanatkumāra said:
Perceiving their gesture and the proper time, the afflicter of the gods,
King Hiraṇyākṣa himself spoke to those enemies of the gods:
'All of you possessors of great māyā, listen together with restraint
to what is timely and wholesome, as pupils to the word of a teacher.
My beloved elder brother, who was to be revered like a father,
was King Hiraṇyakaśipu, high-souled and true to his promise,
righteous, generous, a sacrificer, a giver, endowed with austerity,
one who maintained the sacred fires, master of the four Vedas, bringing happiness to all beings.

For the sake of sovereignty he was slain by the gods, foolish of mind, through deceit.
Because of grief for him I burn and wither, O great asuras,
like a blossoming lotus pulled from the water in summer.
I am able to inflict punishment upon those enemies of the asuras.
I was not ready [before], for the sake of protecting you children here.
I myself, alone, shall go to inflict punishment
upon the enemies of the asuras, without doubt; have no fear, O asuras!'

Hearing that speech of his, those dānavas were filled with joy;
they looked at one another, filled with supreme bashfulness.

and spoke to his brother words that were fully meaningful and gentle:

Then those Dānavas, filled with joy, quickly / harnessed mounts suitable for afflicting the enemy in battle. / 'Make them ready quickly! Let us advance against the deities!' / A tremendous uproar of those mounts arose,
like the roar of the Ocean of Milk stirred by a gentle breeze. / 'This horse is mine! This lion is yours! This leader of elephant herds is mine!
Whose chariot is this, abundantly equipped with instruments of war? / Come, advance with haste! Wait for a moment!
Let all the Daitya lords march forth; we will follow behind. / Mount your chariot, hero! What need have I for a chariot today? / As a foot-soldier alone will I slay the enemies of the gods in battle today!' / Thus there was an exceedingly agreeable clamor among those foes of the gods, / mingled with sounds of flutes and lutes, like the chatter of women.

With three thousand white horses unhindered and swift as thought,
immortal, moving at will, divine, and free from fatigue and distress.
The charioteer of that chariot was known by the name Makarāsilma,
a son of Garutmat, O Vyāsa, a bird moving at will and auspicious.

[Apparatus and page number omitted]
Honored by the shout of "King!" and with blessings,
that king mounted the chariot, as the sun mounts his single-wheeled car.
Wearing armor, having quivers bound, holding arrows, holding a sword, holding a bow,
with the armguard and finger-guards attached, and having a throat-guard made,
adorned with a great banner and an umbrella,
and with many victory flags, he looked like a cloud attended by cranes.
His umbrella then shone above his diadem,
like the moon on a full-moon day having revealed the radiance of clouds.
And his staff-and-skull banner shone as if traversing the sky,
blazing like a risen comet meant for the destruction of the three worlds.

7.8.m:
Just such was the chariot of the son of the great-souled
Andhaka then, O Vyāsa, rumbling like a great rain-cloud.
Then, being told by him, "Go!", the charioteer of the enemy of the gods
urged forward the three thousand excellent horses on the chariot.
Driven on, those swift [horses] endowed with the speed of wind bore him,
moving at will, as the seven horses bear the great chariot of the sun.
In front of him then, Śukra [stood] with a chariot rumbling like a cloud,
appearing like Mercury rising in the sky.
And on his right side stood the dānava Andhaka,
like the sun having reached the southern solstice for the world.
Taking his stand on the other flank was Vipracitti,
like the Himavat, the highest mountain, on the border of the land of Bhārata.
Behind and in front, the other heroic dānavas
marched as they pleased, like planets accompanying the moon.

That army, marching on, looked resplendent as they advanced, O best of sages,
like monsoon clouds accompanied by lightning and thunder at the close [of summer].
With the sounds of horses neighing and the trumpeting of rutting elephants,
with galloping, clapping of arms, shouts, and rising lion-roars, it moved.
Roaring with the sound of musical instruments and lion-roars, with the neighing of horses and the fierce trumpeting of elephants,
resounding with arm-slapping sounds, the terrifying army of the dānavas marched.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, named "The Departure of Hiraṇyākṣa", in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.8.m:
Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana said:
"O venerable one, when the sons of Diti set out for Amarāvatī,
what did the immortals do? I wish to know this.
How did they disappear? What was their counsel and what was their action?
And what counter-response did the gods deliberately prepare?
Righteous, generous, learned, with doubts dispelled,
and dear to all the world—what did the deities do?"
Sanatkumāra said:
"Hear, O Vyāsa, how the gods made a counter-response,
and how, properly armored, they retaliated against what the asuras did.
While the daityas were still setting forth, exceedingly terrible portents,
portending danger for the gods, arose in Amarāvatī.
Meat-eating birds circled overhead on all sides;
the garlands of the gods withered, and an ill-omened odor blew.

"Now the lord of Daityas, Hiraṇyākṣa, the foremost [successor] of Hiraṇyakaśipu, / seeking indeed retribution for his slain brother, / comes forward surrounded by all the chiefs of the Daityas and Dānavas, / accompanied by his sons and grandsons, the lord of Daityas possessing great might and valour.
And his son Andhaka has indeed been made immortal by Brahmā; / he cannot be slain by you, and thence your fear has arisen.
Therefore, well-equipped and fully armoured for battle, / await [him], O great-souled ones, so long as the portents persist."
Hearing his speech, Śakra then said to all the gods: / "Get ready for battle, having resolved your minds.

This great danger has arrived; do not remain without effort. / Let not the lords of Daityas catch us and slay [us] like drunkards, O immortals!"
Then Vāyu, approaching Śakra, the destroyer of all Asuras, / spoke with folded hands in the very assembly of the gods:
"This Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa, surrounded by all the Asuras, / comes to slay the deities, remembering the slaughter of his brother. / Therefore, O mighty one, fully armoured together with us, / arise for victory, O king of the gods, for the destruction of the enemies of the gods!"
Sanatkumāra said:
Then the lord, O great Vyāsa, the king of gods himself, / [put on] an impenetrable divine armour adorned with gold,
Given with sacred formulas according to rule by the son of Aṅgiras himself. / Śakra, whose voice is like cloud-thunder, bound it upon himself. / Resplendent in that armour was glorious Śakra, / like Mount Meru enveloped in clouds with lightning and meteors.

Then the powerful one showed him auspicious signs: / a full jar, weapons, and also Airāvata, / prepared by many divine teachers residing in heaven, / worshipped, perfumed with incense, and made fragrant with mirrors of wrath(?). / Then the god mounted that elephant, / endowed with auspicious marks, four-tusked, dripping with rut. / Mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, the lord then shone / like the rising sun standing upon the peak of the mountain of dawn.
With a white umbrella the king of gods then shone resplendent, / like that king of white mountains with the moon, O great sage! / Fanned by chowries, his radiant face shone / like a full, great autumn lotus fanned by swans. / Beside him stood Jayanta, the righteous son of Śakra, / shining like Kārtikeya, the beloved son of Rudra. / Then the mighty Yama, mounted upon a marked buffalo, / placing the rod of Death before him, [set out] surrounded by ten crores [of attendants].

All the Ādityas went forth, surrounded by twelve akṣauhiṇīs; / and each one of them, O Vyāsa, was a fighter with celestial weapons.
Likewise the Rudras went forth, of great delusion and great strength, / each one then surrounded by sixteen akṣauhiṇīs; / the Vasus with ten, and both the Aśvins with eight; / likewise the divine Āṅgirasas, all of them surrounded by akṣauhiṇīs.
The Yāmas, Dāmas, Sādhyas, and the Lekhas who were of great strength, / they too all assembled together with ten hundred crores.
There were twenty crores of noble Gandharvas, / sixty-four [crores] of serpents, and twenty [crores] of birds;
and fifty crores of Piśācas assembled there. / Of kings [...] noble-souled [...]; / this entire army of the gods was gathered there. / Having seen that supreme, vast, and boundless army of the gods,
The king of pheasants, the foremost knower of righteousness, said: / "O lord, let a battle array be formed, because of those evil-souled ones..."

Therefore, I will form for you a battle array, the Hawk, of extraordinary splendour,
by which you will conquer those Dānavas in battle for some time."
Then that holy Jīva, the great yogin, created a battle array of extraordinary splendour
named the Hawk, promoting the welfare of the gods.
In its neck he placed the lord of wealth [Kubera] and Varuṇa,
as well as Agni, Vāyu, and Jayanta the son of Śakra.
Yama was its crest, as well as both Mṛtyu and Kāla.
Jīva made the Moon and the Sun its mouth and its two eyes.
The twice-born made all the Rudras its one wing,
and the Ādityas its second wing; its centre he made Purandara [Indra].

From our fortune victory will be gained, not otherwise, O bull among gods;
slay the enemies, O mighty-armed one! Let there be no fear for you in battle!"
Then conches, kettledrums, paṭahas, and ḍiṇḍimas,
as well as āḍambaras, nambhas, kṛkavas, and cow-horn trumpets,
mardalas, pepukas, and various musical instruments sounded on every side.
At that sound, there arose great joy for battle among the warriors;
they uttered lion-roars and clapped their arms to instruments.
Then the gods, led by Indra and the foremost deities, desiring victory and eager to slay the foe,
moved forth with conch-shells and mṛdaṅga drums, their hands blazing with unerring weapons of all kinds.
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter named "The Deployment of the Battle Array" in the Skandapurāṇa.

Sanatkumāra said:
When the army of the gods was thus drawn up in battle array, clad in armour and ready for combat,
the dreadful, terrifying host of the Dānavas appeared.
Seeing that army of Dānavas, all the gods with Indra
uttered lion-roars mingled with the sounds of musical instruments.
That exceedingly great roar, O Vyāsa, like that of the churning ocean,
resembling the sound of clouds at the end of a yuga, filled the whole world.
Then all the foremost Dānavas, seeing the chief gods
standing properly arranged in army array, looked at one another.

"Having formed this array, the gods stand as if fearless,
thinking, 'We shall completely conquer the Dānavas in battle.'
Therefore, do you, without delay, form for us an illusory counter-array
suited to break this very array of the gods."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having said, "So be it," he indeed formed the Crescent Moon array,
and sought to cut off the head, body, and other parts of that bird.
At its two horns he placed the two Dānavas Prahlāda and Andhaka;
at the edges, the Nivātakavacas, the Paulomas, and the sons of Kālakā;
Virocana, Bali, and Vipracitti along with his younger brothers,
and the brother of Prahlāda along with the circle of his friends and kinsmen.

[...] / [Bhārgava said:]
"O Hiraṇyākṣa, this is appropriate and wholesome in every way at this time. / For this great battle-array has been formed by you to break the gods' array.
Do what is proper! May good fortune be yours, protected indeed by me! / Protecting one another, all of you wondrous warriors, / do not underestimate at all the gods, who possess great powers of illusion."
Sanatkumāra said:
Then conches, kettledrums, paṇavas, anakas, gomukhas, / āḍambaras, ḍiṇḍimas, and loud paṭahas
and many other kinds [of instruments] by the thousands were sounded, / truly inspiring arrogance and courage in the gods and Dānavas.

7.8.m:
Then, told "Crush them!" by the lords of the Dānavas, / the Dānavas crushed the host of the deities, and struck them on every side.
Those gods too, prepared and endowed with the power of yoga and austerity, / struck the offending Dānavas with diverse weapons.
As swords and the heads of elephants were felled, / there was a terrible, great noise like that of bamboos being split.
As bows were drawn and arrows released, / there was a great roaring sound there like that of mountains cracking apart.
With bhindipālas, spears, and tomara darts flying, / the whole sky became filled as if with fireflies.
With severed heads, feet, and arms, / that battlefield in an instant became uneven and rugged.
With mountain-like elephants, excellent steeds, best of chariots, / and dancing headless trunks, it was terrible to behold in battle.

with diverse neck-protectors, fine silks, and jewels, / with colorful saddle-cloths, and arms adorned with ornaments,
with clubs, spear-shafts, bells, and goads, / the ground there shone like the sky covered with stars.
Enraged, seizing [his foe] by the hair, a mighty chariot-warrior, even though carless, / bounded onto the chariot and forcibly struck down the chariot-fighter.
And there another mighty-armed warrior, striking swiftly at an elephant, / hurled away a chariot with [the fighters] surrounded, as if it were a fistful of kuśa grass at a sacrifice.

7.8.m:
Leaping up from the elephant [when] thrown, [...] / with arrows resembling venomous snakes he dispatched [his foe] to Yama's abode.
Even when he was slain and fallen to the ground, this horse / stood by his rider's feet, as a self-composed disciple waits upon his sleeping guru.
When the warrior and his charioteer were slain, these best horses / carried the chariot, like drunk men [carrying] scripture endowed with knowledge.
Look, another bull among the gods, though tightly bound by a Daitya, / encircled him with his arms and went near the deities.
Look, he cut off the trunk of a charging elephant; / he was struck down on the earth and slain by that very elephant.
This one engaged with one foe was struck by another who arrived; / he too was slain by another god, and that god in turn by yet another.
Many other foot-soldiers, tightly clustered, / bewitched a chariot-warrior and slew him fearlessly.

7.8.m:
[...] / Thus the sky-roaming Siddhas, ṛṣis, and Cāraṇas / praised, took pleasure, smiled, and murmured prayers.
Apsarases carried away the warriors slain there in battle, / and Piśācas rejoiced, and the Nikumbhilas danced.
That battle-music, played with [sounds of] slashing, piercing, and tearing, / became the battle's song, increasing fear in the timid.
With their entire bodies wounded by mutual blows, remembering their enmity, / the gods and asuras, looking like Rākṣasas, then fought, seeking victory for the sake of heaven's sovereignty.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, named "The Battle of the Gods and Asuras", in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.8.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
While that great and terrifying battle was taking place, / the gods then surrounded the Dānavas on all sides.
Death, Time, Yama, Kṛtānta, and Strife, / Treachery, Diseases, Enmity, and mighty Wrath,
and all the hells and Yama's messengers on every side, / and the ghosts and ancestors—these four hosts,
and the god who is Vāmana, and the mighty servants— / all these then entered [the fray] and crushed the Dānava army.
Their limbs broken by Yama's messengers, their chests and shoulders shattered, / the Daityas groaned on the ground like sinners in hells.
Crushed by swords and shields, bound by the nooses of Death, / fallen under Kṛtānta's power, all the sons of Diti were shattered.

And the battle-array of the gods was broken, O son of Śakti! / Then Death (Mṛtyu), Time (Kāla), and the Finisher (Kṛtānta)—those three, / faint with fury, bound Andhaka with many nooses. / But tearing the nooses asunder, that lord of the Daityas, being exceedingly powerful, / mighty as he was, bound Kṛtānta with the noose of his own arms. / Bound by the arm-noose, Kṛtānta, faint with fury, / lifted up Andhaka, and having shaken him, that strong one carried him off by force. / Seeing his son being carried away, Hiraṇyākṣa / struck Kṛtānta very fiercely and firmly with sharp arrows. / That mighty one pierced all his limbs and joints / with sharpened shafts; transfixed by them, he came to a halt.
Seeing him surrounded by arrows, all the gods along with Indra, / raising terrible weapons in their hands, arrived to protect [him].

7.8.m:
"O Śakra, display whatever strength you have; do not delay! / For we are the elder gods, and the entire triple world belongs to us,
by succession of seniority and by right, O best of gods. / But you, having abandoned justice, and having slain my brother,
having become deceitful through [our] trust, attained godhood afterwards. / We here are the elder gods, and you are not gods at all!
As you fight today, I shall take the lives of you all! / Having slain you here today along with your followers, and having offered [you] as an oblation,
I shall become free from debt to my brother who was killed by you through deceit!" / Having spoken thus, drawing his strong bow, the valiant one / pierced [Indra] on the forehead with five sharpened arrows, O Vyāsa.
Pierced by him on the forehead with five arrows, the king of the gods / shone like Mount Meru surrounded by the rays of the sun.
Then, as [Hiraṇyākṣa] was moving about, Śakra cut his bow, / and taking his thunderbolt, he struck him again.

7.8.m: [Vātāpi], Indradamana, Vipāka, and Pāka, / Kālanemi, Ṣaṇḍa, and likewise Amīsṛmuñjika— / each of these he pierced with ten arrows. / And as they drew [their bows] in battle, the swift-handed deity, the Āditya, / severed their bows all at once and let out a roar. / Then against their steeds, divine charioteers, and flags of victory, / as though laughing, O best of brahmins, he struck many blows with his arrows. / With their horses slain, those great archers, their drivers killed everywhere, / drew their swords and all rushed toward Aṃśa with speed. / As they were [rising] like mountains incarnate and roaring like thunderclouds, / the Āditya, unperturbed, filled them with arrows right up to their knees. / Their ankles and knees pierced with shafts, those Dānavas, / abandoning Aṃśa, then fled in haste toward another direction.

7.8.m:
Then the gods raised a great noise of musical instruments, / loud lion-roars, and plenty of arm-slapping sounds. / Lord Aṃśa, having drawn his bow that resembled the rainbow, / wrought a great slaughter among the Dānavas and Daityas.
Aṃśa, the foremost among striking warriors, / felled the heads of the Dānava lords like a wind [shaking down] ripe fruits.
Some, decapitated with arrows by Aṃśa, ran on; / having fled with speed from the battle, they fell lifeless to the ground.
Others of great strength, their arms and thighs cut off, / fell down and groaned terribly like men dwelling in hell.
Their entire limbs covered in arrows, bound in knots of arrows, / they wandered here and there like embodied souls in the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).

7.8.m: There was no mighty Daitya or Dānava there / whom the fierce shafts of the noble-souled Aṃśa did not pierce. / Just as a forest of bandhujīva trees or of aśoka and kiṃśuka trees appears ablaze in flower, / so shone the Daitya army [covered in red blood]. / 'This is Aṃśa! This is Aṃśa!' 'No, not this one—this one!' / Stricken with fear, the Daityas saw everything as consisting of Aṃśa alone. / He, his bow continuously drawn like the sun enveloped in a halo, / pierced each Daitya with winged arrows wherever he saw him. / Neither taking up [an arrow] nor setting it on the string, / nor drawing the bow was Aṃśa seen to do by the Daityas and Dānavas. / His great bow was seen only as a continuous circle; / he appeared in battle then like the midday sun. / Wielding a divine bow, swift-handed and mighty, his bow ever formed into a great circle, / he burned his enemies in battle like fire stirred by the wind [burns] a vast heap of dry fuel. / Thus ends the eighty-first chapter in the [battle narrative of the] Skandapurāṇa.

7.8.m:
Sanatkumāra said: / Seeing those Daitya lords being driven here and there in that manner by Aṃśa, / Bala of great magical power said this to his charioteer: / 'Take me to where this wicked Aṃśa is burning our army, / until with sharp arrows I send him to the abode of Yama.' / Even as he was rushing forward, Aṃśa, the foremost among striking warriors, / severed his flag with an arrow and then his horses one by one.
And with a broad-headed arrow he swiftly brought down the driver's head from his body, / and struck Bala himself on the forehead with five arrows. / Those five arrows shone on the Daitya's forehead / like the rays of the sun emerging from within a dense cloud. / Then the Daitya, an archer, leaped into the sky in anger;

7.8.m:
Just as he did to Aṃśa, he did to other deities as well, / rendering them incapable of effort; that master of great illusion roared aloud. / In some places resembling Bṛhaspati (Gīṣpati), in some places like the sun, / in some places resembling the moon and fire, and in some places equal to planets and stars, / in some places like a mountain, and in some places assuming the form of a vulture, / in some places entering the sky, invisible, he loosed his arrows. / Their limbs crowded with arrows, cut, pierced, and torn open, / the entire army of the gods appeared stunned, as though dumb.
Devoid of the sound of musical instruments, lacking the neighing of horses, / without the trumpeting of elephants, [filled only with] the fierce cries of exhausted warriors, / motionless, that army appeared as if depicted in a painting.

The gods, resplendent as the sun, tormented him with sharp arrows. / Then, being oppressed by the gods, the mighty best of Dānavas,
of fierce prowess, fought with trees born in the forest, O Vyāsa. / Those splendid trees thrown in many ways by Bala then,
the chiefs of the deities sawed through with arrows. Thereupon he approached a mountain, / and seizing a huge peak, filled with deer, wild beasts, and Kinnaras,
he hurled it, raising a tremendous, exceedingly dreadful roar. / As it was thus falling with speed, the powerful Wind forcibly
carried off that peak, and it fell right upon the heads of the Asuras. / Then, one crore of the valiant Dānavas in battle
that mountain peak, released by Bala with a loud roar, crushed. / Seeing those sons of Diti, the Dānavas, slain by that peak,

7.8.m:
"Ho, ho, tigers among Dānavas and Daityas, enemies of the gods! / Why do you flee? Halt! Let there be no fear for you, Dānavas! / Where will you go, Dānavas, and will you find happiness or not? / These gods of great strength, not recognizing their strength formerly, / did not crush those abiding in Pātāla, nor the best of Asuras; / [now] will the lowest of their race destroy you without remainder, even in Pātāla?
Do not go! Turn back! Strive to protect yourselves in every way / by fighting well, Daityas! Have no fear here for your life!
Where has your Danuja-hood gone? Where has your Daitya nature gone? / And where has your enmity with the gods gone? Where has the seizing of the kingdom gone?
That courage, that pride of yours, that lineage and noble birth of yours, / and whatever roaring was yours formerly—the time for that has now arrived!
You said then, 'Daityas, we are not children! / We individually are capable even of destroying the gods!'
